Good night,
brain rot box!

edited by Alina Körber, Marit Duddeck and Tiril Langeland Goodchild

In the meantime it is common knowledge that we should not use our phones right before we are going to bed. Still most of people are doing exactly that. But how bad is this small device really? And what can we do to prevent a bad sleep due to our phones?

SCROLL ↓

It’s 11:42 p.m.

The lights are already turned off.

But a small rectangle still glows in your hand.

Just one more video.

Now it’s already 12:30 and your eyes are burning.

What is happening in our heads?

How do people handle it?

So what now?

Blue-ish light signals daytime to our bodies and can suppress melatonin, our sleep hormone. Even reading on a light-emitting tablet delays melatonin release, compared to a regular printed book.

Sleep is when the brain consolidates memories and processes emotions. Messages, ongoing notifications and emotional content keep the brain alert when it should wind down. Especially for children and teenagers, whose brains are still developing, the stakes are higher. A 2026 JAMA Pediatrics study linked bedtime device use in young people to shorter, poorer sleep. Even though the stakes are higher, long-term evidence is still emerging.

“My phone sleeps next to my pillow. I tell myself I’m just checking the time. Forty minutes later I’m still scrolling.”
Lena
(24-year-old student)
“The phone charges downstairs in the kitchen. Instead I’m using an old-school alarm clock. Before I’m heading upstairs into bed, I’m reading a few pages in current book of choice.”
Susan
(50-year-old office administrator)
“I put on red-tinted glasses every evening around one to two hours before I plan on going to bed. My eyes calm down within minutes. Afterwards I usually fall asleep within 15 minutes. Also I don’t use my phone in bed. The glasses are my signal that the day is over.”
Paul
(22-year-old student)

Evidence for blue-light glasses is mixed. Paul’s calm may owe as much to the ritual as to the lenses. His biggest lever might be that he leaves his phone alone.

An occasional late-night message is not a catastrophe, but the habit matters. So all of us should learn to establish some of them, for example: Keep a screen-free window before bed, use an alarm clock so the phone is not in your bedroom, set Do Not Disturb, with exceptions for real emergencies or even create your own ritual that’s telling your body that the day is over. Whether it’s red glasses or a cup of tea.

Our phones don’t go anywhere. But the bed might be one place they don’t need to follow us. So we need to say: Good night brain rot box!
